evidence: Judged: DRAFT "Think about what you want to do. Are there things you don’t want to do today?" CONTEXT holds it once, as the first two sentences of the paragraph under "Before you begin" (after "Read this page, and the Come all the way back page, when you're awake."). The unchanged "How long do you want to spend on this?", a bracketed aside ("You don't have to do this on a problem. You can do it on something you want to experience more of: love, play, confidence, creativity, communion, whatever.") and "Make sure you're leaving some time at the end to come back, and reflect on what you experienced." follow it. Change check: SOURCE words are "Get clear on what it is you want to do during the induction. What do you want not to do today?"; the draft is Emulate's two sentences with no AI fix, which is what the_change says (what you want to do, and what you don't want to do today). Meaning check against the published guide ("Choose the question or quality you want to explore, what you’re leaving alone today, and how much time you have"): its first two items are kept in order and the third is the unchanged next sentence. Shifts, none a new claim: "Get clear on" becomes "Think about" (a softer verb for the same intention-setting; "Decide to do it" comes later in the section); "during the induction" is dropped, so "what you want to do" is scoped only by context, which is enough here: the heading "Before you begin", "today", and the aside about doing this on a problem or on something you want more of (the guide's "question or quality") all show it is about the session, and the section uses "this" for the practice throughout, so the unchanged "spend on this" still points at the session (a reader who takes it as the thing they want to do gets the same sense); "What do you want not to do today?" becomes the yes/no "Are there things you don’t want to do today?", which still asks the reader to find what they are leaving alone today and drops the stilted "want not to do". No first-person content, named entity, study or fact is added. Reading in context: natural, in the guide's casual voice, and it follows from the "Before you begin" frame; the want / don't-want pair is the guide's own explore / leave-alone distinction and sets what is in and out of today's session, so it is a necessary contrast and not symmetry for its own sake (T12 says not to flag that); "want to" repeats across the three questions because they are parallel items of one checklist. Typography, not a tell: "don’t" is a curly apostrophe and the only one in the whole section (the aside and every other contraction here use straight ones), so it will show as a mismatch next to "You don't" in the same paragraph; suggest a straight one when the card is shown. Tells: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in its paragraph and found none PRESENT. Looked at hardest: T02 (the section is a pre-session checklist, so command, question, question, aside, command is its genre; the draft is the same two beats as the replaced text, the aside and the "whatever" list supply the noticing, and nothing is added), T12 (above), T22 and T06 (two plain prompts, no reassurance, no therapy abstraction; the paragraph also carries reasons and asides), T11 (an opener, but it carries the first of the guide's three steps), T26 (see "want to" above), T13 and T09 (the two D9 pointers: the aside and the closing "leave some time at the end" sentence give the paragraph uneven weight and its own turns), C02 ("what you want to do", "today" and "this" are anchored as above). Linter findings: (1) "B7 short landing at paragraph end": accepted, a false positive in context; the linter saw the draft alone, but in CONTEXT the question is the second of six sentences and the paragraph ends on the longer "Make sure you're leaving some time at the end to come back, and reflect on what you experienced." (2) "D9 follows the source order": accepted; the change swaps two sentences in their own slots, the order is the published guide's, and organization alone is not a tell. (3) "E36/E41 heavy second person" (12.5 you per 100 words): accepted; the draft has two "you", the same as the two sentences it replaces, the guide addresses the reader throughout, and these are the reader's own preparation questions with no reassurance. Side note on the writer's ledger: its T14 and T15 lines say the draft puts back a point Emulate dropped, but this draft is Emulate's own wording with nothing put back, so those two lines are templated; the ABSENT calls are right.
